summary: This standards-track document describes how to convey the path setup type in PCEP messages. A Path Computation Element can compute traffic-engineered paths, which were traditionally set up with RSVP-TE, but other setup methods are possible. It lets PCEP say which method applies.

eli5.summary: A map-maker can say not just which way to go, but also how the trip should be arranged.

questions: how does pcep signal the path setup type
what is the pcep path setup type tlv
what is path setup type capability tlv
subtitle: How PCEP peers announce and select the method used to set up a traffic engineering path, beyond RSVP-TE.

tldr.problem: PCEP and its extensions assumed every traffic engineering path is a label switched path set up with RSVP-TE, even though the PCE architecture allows other setup methods.
tldr.mechanism: Two new TLVs let a PCEP speaker announce the path setup types it supports when a session opens, and tag individual requests, replies, updates and reports with the path setup type to use.
tldr.outcome: One PCEP session can carry several path setup types, and RSVP-TE is the default when nothing is indicated. This RFC defines only the RSVP-TE type and has been updated by RFC 8664.

today: RFC 8408 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8664, so read the two together. It defines only the RSVP-TE path setup type and leaves new types to the documents that introduce them.

sections.title: Beyond RSVP-TE Paths
sections.content:
In PCEP (RFC 5440), a Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) for a path under constraints. The PCE replies with a hop-by-hop path in an Explicit Route Object (ERO), and the PCC uses it to set up the path. RFC 8231 lets a PCC delegate its LSPs to a PCE that can update them, and RFC 8281 lets a PCE instantiate an LSP on a PCC.

All of this assumed paths are label switched and set up with the RSVP-TE signaling protocol. Other setup methods are possible in the PCE architecture, so this document generalizes PCEP to allow them. It defines two new TLVs: PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY, which announces supported setup methods when the session is established, and PATH-SETUP-TYPE, which names the method for a given LSP.

The RFC defines a path setup type code only for RSVP-TE. Any later setup type, and an optional sub-TLV for it, is to be defined by the document that introduces it.
sections.eli5: Until now, everyone assumed there was only one way to build a route. This RFC lets the two sides say which way they mean when there are several.

sections.title: Announcing Capabilities
sections.content:
During session initialization, a PCEP speaker sends an Open message whose OPEN object carries the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV, which has TLV type 34. It holds a Num of PSTs field, a list of one-byte path setup type (PST) values padded with zeros to a multiple of four bytes, and optional sub-TLVs. Each PST has zero or one sub-TLV, and duplicate list entries MUST be ignored. The only PST value defined here is 0, meaning the path is set up using RSVP-TE.

The receiver MUST check the format. Num of PSTs MUST be greater than zero, and the Length field must match the sizes of the list and any sub-TLVs. If the rules are violated, the receiver MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 10 (Reception of an invalid object) and Error-value 11 (Malformed object) and MUST close the session. If an OPEN object has several of these TLVs, all but the first are ignored.

Leaving the TLV out is the same as listing only PST 0 with no sub-TLVs. A speaker MAY omit it if RSVP-TE is the only type it supports, and SHOULD include it if it supports others. A speaker that does not recognize the TLV ignores it, as RFC 5440 requires.
sections.eli5: When two programs say hello, each hands over a list of the building methods it knows. If a list is missing, it is assumed to say only the old standard method.

sections.title: The Path Setup Type TLV
sections.content:
The PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV, TLV type 28, is an optional TLV in the Request Parameters (RP) object and the Stateful PCE Request Parameters (SRP) object. It is four bytes long and holds a reserved field, which MUST be zero, and a one-byte PST field using the same values as the capability TLV.

Its absence means PST 0, so a speaker MAY omit it when the type is RSVP-TE. If an RP or SRP object has more than one such TLV, only the first is processed. A speaker that does not recognize the TLV ignores it and uses RSVP-TE to set up the path.

The reason it matters is that the PCE has to give the path in the right format, and the PCC has to take control-plane and forwarding-plane actions suited to the setup type.
sections.eli5: Each request carries a small label naming the building method. No label means the standard old method.

sections.title: Rules During a Session
sections.content:
At initialization, a speaker that receives the capability TLV MUST assume the peer supports only the listed PSTs. If there is no PST in common, it MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type 21 (Invalid traffic engineering path setup type) and Error-value 2 (Mismatched path setup type) and close the session. If the peer sent no capability TLV, the speaker MUST infer the peer supports at least RSVP-TE.

A PCC sending a PCReq includes the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV in the RP object unless the type is RSVP-TE, and the PCE then uses the matching ERO format in the PCRep. A PCE that does not support the type sends a PCErr with Error-Type 21 and Error-value 1 (Unsupported path setup type) and closes the session. If the PSTs in the PCReq and PCRep do not match, the PCC sends Error-value 2 and closes the session.

For stateful PCEs, a PCUpd or PCInitiate message carries the TLV in the SRP object unless the type is RSVP-TE. A PCC that does not support the type responds with Error-value 1. A PCRpt message from the PCC includes the TLV in its SRP object unless the type is RSVP-TE, and the SRP object MUST be present for any non-RSVP-TE type, even when the SRP-ID-number is the reserved value 0x00000000. A PCRpt triggered by a PCUpd or PCInitiate MUST carry the same PST, or the PCE sends Error-value 2 and closes the session.
sections.eli5: Both sides keep checking they mean the same building method. If they do not, they send an error and stop, rather than building the wrong thing.

sections.title: Manageability Requirements
sections.content:
Networks that mix path setup methods may be harder to configure and observe, and not all devices will support the same set. So every document that adds a new type to the PCEP Path Setup Types registry must include a Manageability Considerations section.

That section must say when devices will use the new type and how operators control it, how the network can be migrated and what backwards-compatibility issues exist, whether paths of the new type are meant to coexist with others over the long term, how operators verify correct operation and which faults must be reported, and whether existing management interfaces such as YANG models need extending. RFC 5706 gives further guidance.
sections.eli5: Anyone who invents a new building method must explain to network operators how to switch to it, run it and check that it works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5440 and RFC 8281 apply, and no additional security measure is required.

The RFC adds one warning. If the security mechanisms of those RFCs are not used, an attacker using a TCP man-in-the-middle attack could inject error messages into the PCEP session when a particular PST is or is not used. That could force a specific PST and might let the attacker attack a weakness in it.
sections.eli5: If the connection is not protected, a sneaky person in the middle could fake errors to push the two sides into using a method that has weak spots.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA allocated TLV types 28 (PATH-SETUP-TYPE) and 34 (PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY) in the PCEP TLV Type Indicators registry.

It also created a sub-registry called PCEP Path Setup Types, with an allocation policy of IETF Review. It starts with one value, 0, for a path set up using RSVP-TE.

Finally, IANA added Error-value 11 (Malformed object) under Error-Type 10 and a new Error-Type 21, Invalid traffic engineering path setup type, with Error-value 1 (Unsupported path setup type) and Error-value 2 (Mismatched path setup type).
sections.eli5: The official number registry got new entries so everyone uses the same numbers for these labels and errors.
